title: Bundibugyo virus outbreak surges as Ebola relative reemerges
summary: Bundibugyo virus, an Ebola relative, has surged in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda with 695 confirmed cases and 138 deaths as of June 11, 2026, surpassing two earlier outbreaks in scale. Limited diagnostic capacity and delays in specimen transport delay isolation and contact tracing in a
takeaways: 695 confirmed cases and 138 deaths as of June 11, 2026
Surpassed Uganda 2007 and DRC 2012 outbreaks in scale and trajectory
Spreads through direct contact with infected bodily fluids
Overlapping symptoms with malaria and typhoid; requires lab confirmation
Scarce laboratory resources in affected DRC regions; samples require long distances to national reference labs
Delays in testing impede isolation and contact tracing

title: Restoring Brain Protein Menin Reverses Signs of Aging in Mice
summary: Scientists found that restoring the brain protein Menin reversed multiple aging signs in mice, including inflammation, cognitive decline, and physical deterioration. The mechanism involves a disrupted chemical pathway where Menin loss reduces D-serine, an amino acid critical for learning and memory.
takeaways: Menin declines with age in the ventromedial hypothalamus, a brain region controlling metabolism
Menin loss triggers lower bone mass, thinner skin, cognitive decline, and shorter lifespan
D-serine, an amino acid, mediates the connection between Menin and cognitive function
Published March 16, 2023, in PLOS Biology by researchers at Xiamen University

title: Kidney Transplant Breakthrough Enables Donation for Previously Impossible Case
summary: A Medical University of Vienna team successfully transplanted a kidney into a 37-year-old patient with zero compatible donors by using teclistamab, a cancer drug, to reduce antibodies against foreign structures. The patient had waited 12+ years with severe HLA sensitization.
takeaways: Patient: 37-year-old, dialysis-dependent, zero probability of donor match (cPRA = 0)
Prior transplants: 2, both failed, causing HLA sensitization
Treatment: teclistamab (cancer medicine) for 31 weeks
Mechanism: eliminates antibody-producing cells in blood and bone marrow
Publication: New England Journal of Medicine; first transplant use of teclistamab

sources.label: Medical University of Vienna / Medical News

title: Axons may naturally resemble strings of pearls, overturning century-old textbook depiction
summary: Johns Hopkins researchers discovered that axons naturally feature pearl-like structures (non-synaptic varicosities) rather than smooth tubes as shown in textbooks for over a century. These repeating bulges influence electrical signal transmission and brain cell signaling.
takeaways: Study published Nature Neuroscience, December 2, 2024
Lead researcher: Shigeki Watanabe, Johns Hopkins associate professor
Pearl-like structures documented in mouse neurons and human brain tissue
Non-synaptic varicosities distinct from larger synaptic varicosities at neurotransmitter sites
Structures influence electrical signal travel; part of normal architecture, not damage

title: FDA Approves First Gene Therapy for Sanfilippo Syndrome Type A
summary: The FDA approved Fayuvi, the first gene therapy specifically designed to treat Sanfilippo syndrome type A, an ultra-rare childhood neurodegenerative disease. The approval provides the first medical treatment option for patients previously without intervention.
takeaways: First FDA-approved treatment for Sanfilippo syndrome type A
Developed by Ultragenyx
Targets ultra-rare childhood neurodegenerative disease (childhood Alzheimer's)

title: Scientists identify immune system overreaction as driver of rapid aging
summary: Researchers at Hebrew University discovered that the immune sensor cGAS triggers rapid aging by mistaking damaged DNA for viral threats. Reducing cGAS activity improved tissue health in fast-aging models, challenging assumptions about DNA damage and cellular decline.
takeaways: cGAS immune sensor confuses damaged DNA with viral threats
Activates chronic sterile inflammation damaging healthy tissue
cGAS also disrupts DNA repair when entering cell nucleus
Reducing cGAS activity improved tissue health across biological systems
Research focused on Ataxia-Telangiectasia and Bloom syndrome

title: Scientists reconstruct videos from mouse brain activity
summary: University College London scientists reconstructed 10-second video clips from neural signals in mice's visual cortex using single-cell recordings and a dynamic neural encoding model. The technique reveals how the brain processes and filters visual information differently from physical stimuli.
takeaways: Reconstructed 10-second videos from mouse visual cortex neurons
Used single-cell recordings rather than broader brain imaging
Dynamic neural encoding model predicted individual neuron responses
Method reveals visual features the brain emphasizes or filters
Published in eLife journal

summary: Ancient DNA analysis reveals Yersinia pestis killed Siberian hunter-gatherers approximately 5,500 years ago, predating the Black Death by millennia. takeaways: Plague detected in prehistoric Lake Baikal remains ~5,500 years ago
40 percent detection rate in 46 individuals tested
Concentrated deaths among children and young teenagers
Published in Nature, led by Ruairidh Macleod (Oxford)

title: Scientists Identify Major Epigenetic Brain Changes Between Ages 50 and 75
summary: Researchers identified major epigenetic and structural brain changes occurring between ages 50 and 75, including sharp decline in embryonically-derived microglia, reduced blood-brain barrier maintenance, and erosion of three-dimensional genome architecture. takeaways: Age window: ages 50–75 shows sharp decline in embryonically-derived microglia
Microglia replaced by cells with pro-inflammatory molecular signatures
Substantial decline in blood-brain barrier maintenance populations
Broad erosion of 3D genome architecture across multiple brain cell types

title: New World Screwworm Parasite Returns to United States After Eradication
summary: The New World screwworm—a flesh-eating parasite eradicated from the U.S. in the 1950s—has returned with confirmed detections in Texas and New Mexico. The parasite poses risks to livestock, wildlife, pets, and rarely humans; researchers developed a tracking dashboard to predict spread using environme
takeaways: Parasite eradicated from U.S. in 1950s; returns with detections in Texas and New Mexico
1950s damage estimate: $50–$100 million annually in U.S. livestock losses
New World screwworm feeds on healthy, living flesh (unlike most fly larvae)
Researchers developed tracking dashboard to predict spread and identify county-level risk
Females lay eggs in open wounds or natural body openings

title: Large review finds calcium and vitamin D supplements provide little fracture prevention benefit in most older adults
summary: A comprehensive review of 69 trials involving nearly 154,000 older adults found that calcium and vitamin D supplements—alone or combined—provide little to no meaningful fracture or fall prevention benefit. The findings challenge routine supplementation recommendations and suggest exercise-based stra
takeaways: 153,902 adults analyzed across 69 randomized controlled trials
High certainty evidence for vitamin D alone (36 trials, 92,045 participants)
High certainty evidence for combination therapy (15 trials, 51,126 participants)
Published in The BMJ
Balance and resistance exercise may be more effective alternatives

title: Scientists Identify Cells That Survive Programmed Death and Rebuild Damaged Tissue
summary: Weizmann Institute scientists identified a population of cells that can initiate apoptosis, survive it, and then rebuild damaged tissue with increased resistance to future injury. The discovery reveals an unexpected role for caspase enzymes in cell survival rather than just cell death.
takeaways: Caspase enzymes can help cells survive programmed death and become more resistant to injury
Mechanism enables rapid tissue repair observed in compensatory proliferation
Published in Nature Communications
Potential concern: cancer cells may exploit this survival mechanism for aggressive regrowth

title: Emergency Medicine Researchers Report Breakthrough in New England Journal of Medicine
summary: A Phase 3 clinical study published in the New England Journal of Medicine found that azithromycin, an antibiotic, did not reduce wheezing-related symptoms better than placebo in preschool children with acute moderate-to-severe wheezing in emergency settings.
takeaways: Study: AZ-SWED (Azithromycin Therapy in Preschoolers with Severe Wheezing)
Finding: azithromycin no more effective than placebo for symptom reduction
Population: preschool-age children, moderate-to-severe acute wheezing
Funding: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI)
Publication context: NEJM receives 16,000 submissions/year, accepts ~5%

title: Hidden immune organ in skull discovered to fight brain cancer in mice

Contain organized immune structures including T follicular helper cells supporting antibody production

summary: University of Louisville researchers identified urolithin A (UroA), a compound produced by gut bacteria when digesting pomegranates, walnuts, and berries, as a potential treatment for inflammatory bowel disease. takeaways: Compound: urolithin A (UroA), produced during digestion of pomegranates, walnuts, berries

title: Study identifies optimal whole grain intake of 4-6 servings daily for heart health
summary: A meta-analysis of 87 randomized controlled trials found that consuming 4–6 servings of whole grains daily (60–100 grams dry weight) produces the strongest improvements in cardiovascular risk factors including cholesterol, blood pressure, and inflammation.

60–100 grams per day (dry weight)
Improvements in weight, cholesterol, LDL, triglycerides, blood glucose
Benefits observed at 30–40 grams but plateau at higher levels
Meta-analysis of 87 clinical trials, over 6,500 participants

takeaways: Erucamide is naturally occurring eye molecule that protects retina
Activates protective immune and cellular responses
Functions as signaling molecule coordinating retinal cells
Published June 19, 2026 in Nature Neuroscience
May lead to treatments for diabetic retinopathy, retinitis pigmentosa, macular degeneration

Reduced kidney-related death and complication risk
